summary: Implemented HttpToolDownloader with 64 KB progress reporting, atomic temp→destination write, and full cancellation propagation. Added Microsoft.Extensions.Http to Infrastructure.csproj. 3 new integration tests (AC1-AC3) pass; 85 total tests pass with no regressions.

comments.note: The WP scope described 'in-process Kestrel canned blob'. The ConfigureKestrel extension method is not accessible on ConfigureWebHostBuilder in non-Web SDK projects even with <FrameworkReference Include='Microsoft.AspNetCore.App' />. A custom HttpMessageHandler provides equivalent test coverage (no external network, byte-exact assertions, progress and cancellation) without requiring the Web SDK. The approach is well-established for HttpClient unit/integration testing.

SyncProgress<T> avoids the thread-pool scheduling delay of Progress<T>, making progress assertions deterministic. This pattern is worth documenting in a shared test utilities class if the test surface grows.

The Infrastructure.Tests project targets net10.0 while VideoIndexer.Tests targets net8.0. This mismatch may cause issues if shared test utilities are ever extracted. Consider aligning TFMs or creating a shared test helpers project.

metrics.test_coverage: 3 new tests: byte-exact AC1, monotonic progress AC2, cancellation+no-leftover-file AC3

comments.note: No null-guard on 'url' or 'destinationPath' parameters. Nulls propagate to HttpClient.GetAsync or FileStream constructor, yielding ArgumentNullException. Acceptable given callers are expected to supply valid values.

If the destination directory does not exist, FileStream creation throws DirectoryNotFoundException, caught by the catch block (no temp file to delete). Exception propagates correctly; callers must ensure directory exists. Not documented in interface but low-risk.

AC text states IProgress<long> but both IToolDownloader and implementation use IProgress<ProvisioningProgress>. The test verifies BytesReceived is monotonically non-decreasing, satisfying the spirit of the AC. No failure — doc/AC text is slightly stale.

Cancellation test uses a pre-cancelled token caught immediately in CannedResponseHandler.SendAsync before the FileStream is opened. Cancellation mid-stream (after FileStream open) is not explicitly tested, but the catch block deletes the temp file on any exception, including OperationCanceledException, so mid-stream cleanup is covered by code review of the implementation.

summary: Reviewed 4 files (HttpToolDownloader.cs, VideoIndexer.Infrastructure.csproj, HttpToolDownloaderTests.cs, IToolDownloader.cs). 0 Critical, 0 High, 2 Medium (SSRF/A10 and path-overwrite/A03), 2 Low, 0 Info. No blocking findings. Security sign-off: PASS.

comments.note: [Medium] A10 — SSRF: 'url' parameter is passed directly to HttpClient.GetAsync() with no URL scheme validation, no hostname allowlist, and no RFC-1918 block. File: HttpToolDownloader.cs, line 35. In the provisioning context the URL is application-configured, but the IToolDownloader interface is general-purpose. Remediation: (1) validate that url.StartsWith('https://') before issuing the request; (2) document at the interface level that callers must not pass user-controlled URLs without explicit allowlisting.

[Medium] A03 — Path Traversal / Arbitrary File Overwrite: 'destinationPath' is not canonicalized before use. File.Move(tempPath, destinationPath, overwrite: true) at HttpToolDownloader.cs line 101 can overwrite arbitrary files if destinationPath is attacker-controlled. In the provisioning context paths are application-constructed, mitigating this in practice. Remediation: callers should call Path.GetFullPath() and validate the result is within an expected base directory before passing to DownloadAsync; consider using overwrite: false and pre-deleting if replacement is intentional.

[Low] A05 — Predictable Temp File Path: temp file is named destinationPath + '.tmp'. File: HttpToolDownloader.cs, line 45. On shared systems a symlink placed at that path before the download starts could redirect the write. Low risk given app-controlled paths in provisioning context. Remediation: use Path.GetTempFileName() for the temp path rather than appending '.tmp', or ensure the parent directory is not world-writable.

[Low] A09 — Logging Gap: no audit logging of the download URL, destination path, bytes received, or completion/failure. This component downloads and writes executables (ffmpeg); absence of an audit trail makes it harder to detect supply-chain substitution or unexpected downloads. Remediation: inject ILogger<HttpToolDownloader> and log (at Information) URL+destination at start and bytes-received at completion; log (at Warning/Error) any exception before re-throw.

CancellationToken: correctly propagated through all async call sites (GetAsync, ReadAsStreamAsync, ReadAsync, WriteAsync, FlushAsync). Catch block deletes temp on OperationCanceledException before re-throwing. No silent swallowing. No issues.

summary: Code review passed. HttpToolDownloader is well-implemented: ResponseHeadersRead streaming, 64 KB buffer, atomic temp->dest promotion, catch-all cleanup, final guaranteed progress report, ConfigureAwait(false) throughout. Tests use a clean in-process CannedResponseHandler with no external network access. One documentation-forward recorded for IToolDownloader interface exception tags.

comments.note: [documentation-forward] IToolDownloader.DownloadAsync interface method is missing <exception cref='HttpRequestException'> and <exception cref='OperationCanceledException'> XML doc tags. These exceptions are documented on the concrete implementation via inheritdoc extensions, but the interface contract should declare them directly so consumers know what to expect without inspecting the implementation.

HttpCompletionOption.ResponseHeadersRead is used correctly for streaming. Atomic temp->destination promotion pattern (File.Move overwrite:true) is idiomatic and correct. Final unconditional progress report ensures callers always receive at least one callback — a nice design touch. ConfigureAwait(false) applied consistently throughout.
